claim: When customers are in two geographic locations, Cross-Region Replication can minimize latency by keeping object copies in AWS Regions that are geographically closer to the users.
question: When does Cross-Region Replication help latency rather than compliance?

evidence.quote: **Minimize latency** – If your customers are in two geographic locations, you can minimize latency in accessing objects by maintaining object copies in AWS Regions that are geographically closer to your users.

claim: Replication can put replicas directly into S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, S3 Glacier Deep Archive or another storage class in the destination bucket; or it can keep the same class and let a lifecycle configuration on the destination move replicas to a colder class as they age.
question: Can a replica be stored in a cheaper storage class than its source object?

values.display: directly put objects into S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, S3 Glacier Deep Archive, or another storage class

evidence.quote: **Replicate objects into different storage classes** – You can use replication to directly put objects into S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval, S3 Glacier Deep Archive, or another storage class in the destination buckets. You can also replicate your data to the same storage class and use lifecycle configurations on the destination buckets to move your objects to a colder storage class as they age.

claim: With the owner override option, replication changes replica ownership to the AWS account that owns the destination bucket, whoever owns the source object; this can be used to restrict access to the replicas.
question: How can a replica in another account be owned by that account instead of the source owner?

evidence.quote: **Maintain object copies under different ownership** – Regardless of who owns the source object, you can tell Amazon S3 to change replica ownership to the AWS account that owns the destination bucket. This is referred to as the *owner override* option. You can use this option to restrict access to object replicas.

claim: To fail over to a bucket in another Region and keep all metadata and objects in sync, set up two-way (bi-directional) replication rules before configuring Multi-Region Access Point failover controls, so data written to the failover bucket is replicated back to the source bucket.
question: What must be in place before Multi-Region Access Point failover so that no writes are lost on failback?

qualifiers.scope: S3 Replication with Multi-Region Access Points
qualifiers.condition: failover with Multi-Region Access Point failover controls

evidence.quote: **Replicate objects and fail over to a bucket in another AWS Region** – To keep all metadata and objects in sync across buckets during data replication, use two-way replication (also known as bi-directional replication) rules before configuring Amazon S3 Multi-Region Access Point failover controls. Two-way replication rules help ensure that when data is written to the S3 bucket that traffic fails over to, that data is then replicated back to the source bucket.
